title: AI's Architects Are Warning That Their Own Creation Could Collapse the Industry That Built It
excerpt: Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman have separately forecast mass job losses and software company failures — and India's army of coders is listening
body:
In the space of a single week, the two most consequential warnings about artificial intelligence came not from sceptics or regulators, but from the men building it. Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic — the company behind the Claude AI model, now valued at nearly $900 billion — declared that software would soon become "cheap, maybe essentially free," and that SaaS companies whose competitive advantage rests on the complexity of their code could "go bust." Hours later, Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft's head of AI, predicted that most white-collar jobs — lawyers, accountants, middle managers — would be "fully automated within 12 to 18 months."

These are not marginal figures issuing dystopian tweets for attention. Amodei and Suleyman sit at the apex of an industry that controls the trajectory of the global economy. When they speak about the future of work, they are describing the products their own companies are building. The effect is something like a tobacco executive warning about lung cancer — alarming precisely because the source has no incentive to exaggerate.

## The Indian dimension

For India, the stakes of these predictions are existential in a way they are not for most other countries. The Indian technology services industry — Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL, and their constellation of smaller peers — employs more than five million people and accounts for roughly 8% of GDP. That industry was built on a simple arbitrage: skilled Indian engineers could write, maintain, and test software more cheaply than their Western counterparts. If AI reduces the cost of software production to near zero, the arbitrage evaporates.

The threat is not hypothetical. Amodei has claimed that AI will write "100% of code within a year." Even if the timeline is optimistic by a factor of three, the direction is unambiguous. Entry-level coding jobs — the traditional on-ramp for hundreds of thousands of Indian engineering graduates each year — are the most immediately vulnerable. The Indian IT industry has already begun shedding entry-level positions; campus hiring by the majors fell by double digits in FY26.

## Silicon Valley's Indian workforce in the crosshairs

The implications extend far beyond Bangalore. More than 300,000 Indian workers in the United States hold H-1B visas, the vast majority in technology roles. For this cohort, the AI disruption carries a uniquely cruel double bind: lose your job, and you lose your right to remain in the country. The six-year visa clock does not pause for retraining.

Suleyman's prediction about white-collar automation is particularly relevant for the growing number of Indian-origin professionals who have moved beyond coding into finance, consulting, and corporate management — roles that AI agents are increasingly capable of performing end-to-end. Microsoft's own Copilot product already handles tasks from drafting legal memos to analysing spreadsheets, functions that employed thousands of Indian professionals at firms from Deloitte to McKinsey.

## The paradox of growth

Amodei frames the situation as a paradox: AI could simultaneously produce "very high GDP growth and very high unemployment." For India, this paradox is particularly stark. The country is the world's largest user of ChatGPT's image generation tools; Indian startups are among the fastest adopters of AI coding assistants. The technology that threatens Indian jobs is also the technology that Indian firms are most enthusiastically embracing.

This is not a contradiction so much as a race. The companies and workers who integrate AI into their workflows earliest will survive; those who treat it as a distant threat will not. Zoho's Sridhar Vembu, one of India's most respected tech founders, recently flagged this uncomfortable truth: AI is writing more code, but the software is not getting better. The implication is that productivity gains from AI may accrue to capital, not labour — a dynamic that would widen inequality in a country already struggling with jobless growth.

## What comes next

The honest answer is uncertainty. The same AI executives who predict mass displacement are also the ones investing billions in training programmes and partnerships designed to create new categories of work. Anthropic and Microsoft both maintain that AI will "augment" rather than replace most roles — a position that becomes harder to defend with every product launch.

For India's diaspora, the message is uncomfortably clear: the technology industry that lifted millions of Indian families into the global middle class is about to be reshaped by the very tools it helped create. Whether that reshaping is a catastrophe or an opportunity depends entirely on how fast India — its government, its companies, and its workers — can adapt. The clock, as Suleyman might put it, is already ticking.
